Specifically, revenue from company-operated stores and other retail locations is recognized at the point of sale, while e-commerce revenue, sales to wholesale accounts, and in-home fitness hardware sales are recognized upon receipt by the customer [1][2]. In certain arrangements where payment is received before the customer receives the promised good, these payments are initially recorded as deferred revenue and recognized as revenue only when control transfers to the customer [1][2]. All revenue is reported net of markdowns and discounts, sales taxes collected on behalf of taxing authorities, and returns, with an allowance recognized for estimated returns [1][2]. Additionally, shipping fees billed to customers are recorded as revenue in the same period as the related revenue, and proceeds from gift card sales are deferred and recognized as revenue when the gift card is redeemed [2].

A significant portion of its private brand and non-consumable business suppliers are located in China, exposing the company to risks from political and economic instability, labor problems, currency exchange rates, tariffs, trade restrictions, and disruptions from events like natural disasters or public health crises, any of which could materially affect its business, financial condition, and results of operations [4]. The company also purchases significant amounts of products from suppliers with limited supply capabilities, and there is no assurance existing suppliers can accommodate anticipated growth or continue supplying at preferential prices; Chewy notes it has already experienced disruptions from existing suppliers being unable to supply products in a timely or cost-effective manner [8]. If key suppliers discontinue selling to Chewy or discontinue preferential pricing or exclusive incentives, this could negatively impact the business, and it can be challenging to persuade customers to switch products if a supplier is lost [8]. Chewy also warns that if it cannot identify new suppliers or replace lost ones, it may face a competitive disadvantage and business disruption [6][8]. Additionally, reduction or discontinuance of supplier incentives such as trade allowances and cooperative advertising funds could reduce profitability, and if suppliers offer preferential pricing to competitors instead, Chewy's competitive advantage could suffer [6]. Finally, Chewy notes risks tied to product safety and quality control, since it depends on suppliers—including private brand manufacturers—to comply with product safety laws, and failures could lead to recalls, litigation, or loss of consumer confidence [7].
